questions.question: Around the 8th to 10th century, a group of Zoroastrians fleeing Greater Khorasan landed on the coast of Gujarat. Legend says the local king, Jadi Rana, sent them a brimming pot of milk to indicate his land was full. Their high priest stirred in a spoonful of sugar to promise they would sweeten the kingdom without displacing anyone. By what name is the community that grew from this landing now known?
questions.explanation: The migrants named their first settlement Sanjan after a town in Khorasan; their descendants came to be called Parsis, from Pars/Persia.

questions.question: In a quiet village in coastal Gujarat sits the holiest fire of Indian Zoroastrians, kept continuously burning since long before the temple itself was consecrated in 1742. Pilgrims travel from Mumbai, Karachi and even Yazd to pay respects to this sacred flame. Name the village.
questions.explanation: The Udvada Atash Behram houses the Iranshah, the oldest continuously burning Zoroastrian fire in India.

questions.question: Born in 1839 to a family of Parsi priests in Navsari, this man dreamed of an Indian steel industry, a hydroelectric plant and a science institute, but only lived to see the first of his great projects open in 1903 — the Taj Mahal hotel in Bombay. Name him.
questions.explanation: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata, the founder of the Tata Group, was born into a Parsi mobed family in Navsari.

questions.question: He was born in Paris in 1904 to a Parsi father and a French mother, became India's first licensed pilot in 1929, and the airline he founded in 1932 was nationalised in 1953 to become Air India. Name him.
questions.explanation: Jehangir Ratanji Dadabhoy Tata received the first pilot's licence issued in India and is called the father of Indian civil aviation.

questions.question: In 1897, in a small shed near the Bombay Gas Works, two Parsi brothers began making locks that they claimed could defeat the best burglars in the world. They went on to make safes, soaps made from vegetable oil, and refrigerators that became fixtures in middle-class Indian homes. Which family business did they found?
questions.explanation: Ardeshir and Pirojsha Godrej started with springless locks in 1897 and built one of India's most recognisable Parsi-owned conglomerates.

questions.question: In 1736 a Parsi master shipwright from Surat moved to Bombay to build docks and warships for the East India Company. The textile arm of the dynasty he founded still produces bedsheets that almost every Indian household knows. Which Parsi business family?
questions.explanation: Lovji Nusserwanjee Wadia laid the foundation; his descendants built Bombay Dyeing and the wider Wadia Group.

questions.question: His father bought a small stake in Tata Sons in the 1930s; by 2011 he was the single largest individual shareholder in India's biggest conglomerate, with construction interests stretching from the Brabourne Stadium to the Sultan of Oman's palace. The Irish-Indian Parsi businessman was nicknamed the Phantom of Bombay House. Name him.
questions.explanation: Pallonji Mistry chaired the Shapoorji Pallonji group and held about 18 percent of Tata Sons at his peak.

questions.question: Born in Bombay in 1909 to a wealthy Parsi family, he set up TIFR in 1945 and the Atomic Energy Establishment at Trombay in 1954, and is universally called the father of India's nuclear programme. Name him.
questions.explanation: Homi Jehangir Bhabha, a Parsi physicist, shaped India's three-stage nuclear plan; the Trombay centre was renamed BARC after him.

questions.question: In 1973 he became the first Indian officer ever promoted to Field Marshal, two years after orchestrating the 12-day campaign that liberated Bangladesh. Famously, when Indira Gandhi pressed him to attack East Pakistan in spring 1971, he replied that he would only do so when he was ready. Name this Parsi soldier.
questions.explanation: Sam Hormusji Framji Jamshedji Manekshaw, known as Sam Bahadur, came from a Parsi family that had moved from Gujarat to Amritsar.

questions.question: Born in 1866 to a Parsi family that had converted to Christianity, she became the first woman to study law at Oxford and the first female advocate in India, spending much of her career fighting for purdahnashin women whom no male lawyer could meet. Name her.
questions.explanation: Cornelia Sorabji also became the first woman to graduate from Bombay University and worked as legal adviser to the Court of Wards in Bengal.

questions.question: He was born in Zanzibar in 1946 to Parsi parents from Gujarat, sent at age eight to St Peter's, a British-style boarding school in the Maharashtra hill town of Panchgani, and would later front one of the biggest rock bands in history under a stage name. By what name do we know Farrokh Bulsara?
questions.explanation: The Queen frontman kept his Zoroastrian funeral rites; his sister has spoken of his pride in his Parsi-Gujarati roots.

questions.question: Born in Bombay in 1936 to a Parsi family — his father Mehli founded the Bombay Symphony Orchestra — he went on to lead the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the New York Philharmonic and the Israel Philharmonic. Name this conductor.
questions.explanation: Zubin Mehta, now Music Director Emeritus of the Israel Philharmonic, is among the most decorated conductors of the last half-century.

questions.question: Before turning to films in his late thirties, this Parsi from Mumbai sold wafers at Grant Road station and worked as a waiter at the Taj. He is now better known as Dr Asthana in Munna Bhai MBBS and the principal Viru Sahastrabuddhe — Virus — in 3 Idiots. Name him.
questions.explanation: Boman Irani, born in 1959 to an Irani Zoroastrian family, became one of Hindi cinema's most reliable character actors.

questions.question: The last male Parsi to play cricket for India, this flamboyant wicket-keeper-batsman from Bombay shared a Lancashire dressing room with Clive Lloyd through much of the 1970s and helped them lift the Gillette Cup four times. Name him.
questions.explanation: Farokh Engineer played 46 Tests for India between 1961 and 1975 and nine seasons at Lancashire.

questions.question: From Akbar in the late 16th century right down to Bahadur Shah Zafar in 1857, the official court language of the Mughal empire — used for revenue records, diplomatic letters and court poetry — was not Hindi, Urdu or Turkish. Which language?
questions.explanation: Akbar formalised Persian as the language of administration; it remained so until the British replaced it with English and vernaculars in the 1830s.

questions.question: Between 1589 and 1596, Abul Fazl finished a vast Persian work in three volumes describing the reign of his patron — the third volume, a kind of administrative gazetteer, lists everything from imperial revenue to the prices of vegetables and the rules of polo. Name this third volume.
questions.explanation: The Ain-i-Akbari forms the third volume of Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and is our richest source on Akbar's administration.

questions.question: Shah Jahan's eldest son, an unabashed mystic, gathered Sanskrit pandits in Delhi and in 1657 produced a Persian translation of fifty Upanishads. He called the work Sirr-i-Akbar, the Greatest Mystery, and argued that this was the hidden book the Quran spoke of. Name this prince.
questions.explanation: Dara Shikoh's Sirr-i-Akbar later reached Europe via a Latin translation and shaped Schopenhauer's reading of Indian thought.

questions.question: Babur wrote his frank, gossipy autobiography in his Central Asian mother tongue Chagatai Turkish, but his grandson Akbar had it translated into the language of his court. By what name is this autobiography of the founder of the Mughal dynasty known?
questions.explanation: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan produced the Persian translation of the Baburnama in 1589 for Akbar's library.

questions.question: Jahangir followed his great-grandfather's example and wrote his own memoirs in Persian, recording everything from his sightings of dodos to his honest admission of his addictions. By what Persian name is this autobiography known?
questions.explanation: Also called the Jahangirnama, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri is admired for its candour and natural-history detail.

questions.question: Born in 1253 in Patiyali, this disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya fused Persian, Arabic, Turkic and Indian musical traditions to create qawwali, mixed Persian with the local Hindavi in playful poems like Zeehal-e-Miskeen, and earned the nickname Tuti-e-Hind, the Parrot of India. Name him.
questions.explanation: Khusrau died in Delhi in 1325 and lies buried near his pir's shrine at Nizamuddin.

questions.question: This 17th-century Sufi from Delhi wrote a famously dense, difficult Persian — so layered that there is still a saying in Kabul and Dushanbe that you cannot understand him properly until your beard is white. To this day he is read more in Tajikistan and Afghanistan than in his own city. Name this Indo-Persian poet.
questions.explanation: Abdul-Qadir Bedil (1642-1720) lived and died in Delhi but became the patron poet of the Persianate world east of Iran.

questions.question: He wrote more than 11,000 verses in Persian and only a slim divan in Urdu, and once told his readers to look at his Persian work for its colourful pictures and to pass over his Urdu collection as a mere sketch. Yet it is the Urdu ghazals of this Delhi poet that the subcontinent now sings. Name him.
questions.explanation: Ghalib valued his Persian work above his Urdu, but it is the Urdu divan that became canonical after his death in 1869.

questions.question: Of the roughly 12,000 verses written by this Sialkot-born thinker, around 7,000 are in Persian — including Asrar-i-Khudi and Payam-i-Mashriq, his answer to Goethe's West-Eastern Divan. In Iran he is so revered that even Ayatollah Khamenei has praised his Persian poetry. Name him.
questions.explanation: Iqbal's Persian work made him a household name in Iran, where his verses were recited during the 1979 revolution.

questions.question: The last Mughal — exiled to Rangoon after 1857 — was himself a respected poet who wrote ghazals in both Urdu and Persian and gathered around him Ghalib, Zauq and Momin. Name this poet-emperor.
questions.explanation: Bahadur Shah II took the pen name Zafar; his lament Lagta nahin hai jee mera was written in exile in Burma.

questions.question: In February 1739, a former sheep-herder turned shah of Iran routed the Mughal army at Karnal, occupied Delhi, and a month later ordered a massacre that killed tens of thousands. Name this Persian invader of India.
questions.explanation: Nadir Shah Afshar's 1739 sack of Delhi shattered Mughal prestige and effectively ended Mughal power outside the Doab.

questions.question: Which fabulously gem-encrusted throne — commissioned by Shah Jahan, inaugurated in 1635 after seven years of work, and carried off to Iran in 1739 as war loot — gives its name to the dynasty that later ruled Iran until 1979?
questions.explanation: The Takht-i-Tavus was looted by Nadir Shah; in modern times, Pahlavi shahs of Iran were said to sit on the Peacock Throne.

questions.question: After Nadir Shah's 1739 invasion, this great diamond — set into the Peacock Throne by Shah Jahan — went briefly to Iran, then to Afghanistan, was won back by Ranjit Singh, and was finally surrendered to the British after the annexation of Punjab. Name the diamond.
questions.explanation: Koh-i-Noor means Mountain of Light in Persian; it now sits in the Crown of Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in the Tower of London.

questions.question: When Mumtaz Mahal died in childbirth in 1631, Shah Jahan summoned a board of architects to design her tomb. Most historians credit the overall plan to the emperor's chief architect, who later supervised the Red Fort in Delhi. Name this architect of the Taj Mahal.
questions.explanation: Ustad Ahmad Lahauri led a multinational team that included Persian and Ottoman specialists in calligraphy, gardens and domes.

questions.question: After Humayun died in 1556, his widow Bega Begum commissioned a tomb in Delhi from a Persian architect she summoned from Herat. The double-domed result became the prototype for the Taj. Name this architect.
questions.explanation: Mirak Mirza Ghiyas died before Humayun's Tomb was finished in 1572; his son Sayyed Muhammad completed it.

questions.question: The Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb and Babur's own garden in Kabul all share a single Persian quadripartite garden layout, with four water channels meeting at a central pool to symbolise the four rivers of Paradise. What is this layout called?
questions.explanation: Charbagh literally means four-garden; Babur is credited with introducing it from Iran to the Indian subcontinent.

questions.question: Mughal miniature painting really begins when Humayun, returning from his exile at the court of Shah Tahmasp, brought two great Persian masters back to Delhi: Abd al-Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali. They had been trained in which Persian dynasty's royal atelier?
questions.explanation: The Safavid Tabriz school under Shah Tahmasp shaped the early Mughal atelier that Akbar later expanded.

questions.question: Jahangir, an obsessive naturalist, kept one court painter on a tight leash because he was the only one who could capture a turkey, a zebra or a Himalayan pheasant with the right scientific accuracy. The emperor gave him the title Nadir-ul-Asr, the Wonder of the Age. Name this painter.
questions.explanation: Ustad Mansur's bird, animal and flower studies for Jahangir are now considered the apex of Mughal natural-history painting.

questions.question: The dynasty that ruled Awadh from the 1720s came originally from the Iranian city of Nishapur and brought with them their Twelver Shia faith and a love of Persian arts and food, transforming Lucknow and Faizabad. By what title were these rulers known?
questions.explanation: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk, the first Nawab, was a Sayyid from Nishapur in eastern Iran.

questions.question: Begun in 1780 by a Nawab of Awadh as a famine-relief project, this great Lucknow building employed labourers by day and noblemen by night for almost a decade, and houses a vast central hall along with the maze-like Bhulbhulaiya. Name the building.
questions.explanation: Asaf-ud-Daula built the Bara Imambara between 1780 and 1784 to provide work during a brutal famine.

questions.question: Born in 1800, this Lucknow poet is said to have composed more than ten thousand marsiyas — elegies on the martyrs of Karbala — turning a religious form of Persian origin into the bedrock of serious Urdu poetry. Name him.
questions.explanation: Mir Babar Ali Anees is regarded as the supreme marsiya poet of Urdu, drawing on a tradition rooted in Shia Iran.

questions.question: Kitab for book, qalam for pen, kursi for chair, darvaza for door, bazaar for market, dost for friend, dushman for enemy. From which single language did Hindi-Urdu borrow all of these everyday words?
questions.explanation: Persian was the prestige and administrative language of north India for centuries, leaving a thick layer of loanwords in Hindustani.

questions.question: When a north Indian says goodbye with Khuda hafiz, gestures at the aasmaan, calls life zindagi or thanks you with shukriya, which language is doing the heavy lifting?
questions.explanation: Khuda, aasmaan, zindagi and shukriya are all classic Persian loanwords absorbed into Hindi-Urdu vocabulary.

questions.question: The biryani of Hyderabad and Awadh probably gets its very name from a Persian word that simply means to fry or to roast, applied to a phrase that literally translates as fried rice. What is that Persian root word?
questions.explanation: The Persian phrase birinj biryan, fried rice, gives both the name and the basic technique of biryani.

questions.question: Crisp, triangular, deep-fried and stuffed — the everyday Indian street snack we call by one name was already being praised by Amir Khusrau around 1300, who called it by its Persian original. From which Persian word does the name samosa derive?
questions.explanation: The Middle Persian sambosag, a triangular pastry, gave Hindi-Urdu samosa and Arabic sambusak.

questions.question: The bright orange, syrup-soaked Indian sweet eaten at every wedding and on every Independence Day morning takes its name from a Persian word that turns into the Arabic zulabiya in 10th-century cookbooks. Which Indian sweet?
questions.explanation: The Persian zolbiya and Arabic zulabiya are both attested in medieval cookbooks; the dish reached India by the late medieval period.

questions.question: A tall glass of vermicelli noodles, sweet basil seeds, milk, rose syrup and sometimes a scoop of kulfi — a staple of Bombay and Hyderabad ice-cream parlours, it descends directly from the Persian rose-and-vermicelli sorbet faloodeh. Name the Indian dessert.
questions.explanation: Faloodeh is the Persian original, made of thin frozen noodles, rose syrup and lemon; the Indo-Pak falooda adds milk and kulfi.

questions.question: Persian pilav, Awadhi pulao, Hyderabadi yakhni pulao, Kashmiri pulao — all are versions of a rice-and-stock dish that the Mughals brought from Iran and Central Asia. What is the family name of this technique, attested in Persian since at least the 10th century?
questions.explanation: Pilaf, pulao and pilav are regional names for the same Persian technique of cooking rice in spiced stock.

questions.question: The cool sweet drinks of an Indian summer — rose, khus, badam, bel — are still called by a Persian word that English then borrowed twice over, once as the soft drink and once as the frozen dessert. What is the Persian word?
questions.explanation: From sharbat we get both sherbet and the cocktail-bar sorbet, and in India the whole family of rose, khus and almond drinks.

questions.question: The soft, slightly sweet flatbread of Awadhi cuisine, baked in a tandoor and brushed with milk and saffron — a Lucknow specialty whose name simply means milk-bread in Persian. Name it.
questions.explanation: Sheer means milk and maal means rubbed in Persian; sheermal is one of the breads the Awadhi nawabs popularised in Lucknow.

questions.question: Skewered, marinated and grilled — the family of meats that Indians call kebab takes its very name from a word that travelled along with cooks from Iran and Central Asia. Seekh, shami, galouti, boti — what is the umbrella term?
questions.explanation: Kebab entered Hindi-Urdu from Persian-Arabic and now covers everything from Lucknowi galouti to Punjabi seekh.

questions.question: In May 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani and Afghan President Ashraf Ghani signed a trilateral transit agreement around an Iranian deep-water port, giving India sea-and-land access to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. Name the port.
questions.explanation: Chabahar, on the Gulf of Oman in southeastern Iran, is roughly 800 km closer to Afghanistan than Pakistan's Karachi port.

questions.question: Linking Mumbai to Bandar Abbas, on to the Caspian, then up through Russia to St Petersburg — the multimodal trade corridor that India, Iran and Russia have promoted since 2000 is meant to cut shipping times to Europe roughly in half. Name this corridor, often abbreviated INSTC.
questions.explanation: The INSTC was conceived in 2000 by India, Iran and Russia as an alternative to the Suez Canal route to Europe.

questions.question: Discovered by ONGC Videsh in 2008 in the Persian Gulf, this giant Iranian gas field — whose name carries a B for the block — became the subject of long, frustrating negotiations between Delhi and Tehran throughout the 2010s. Name the field.
questions.explanation: Farzad-B was discovered by ONGC Videsh in 2008 but its development contract was eventually given to an Iranian company in 2021.

questions.question: K Asif spent more than a decade and famously bankrupted several producers making a 1960 Hindi epic set in Akbar's court, with Madhubala as the courtesan Anarkali, Dilip Kumar as Prince Salim and a young Lata singing Pyaar Kiya Toh Darna Kya. Name the film.
questions.explanation: Mughal-e-Azam premiered in 1960 and stands as the towering Hindi-cinema portrait of the Persian-speaking Mughal court.

questions.question: Ashutosh Gowariker's 2008 historical drama paired Hrithik Roshan as the Persian-speaking third Mughal emperor with Aishwarya Rai as a Rajput princess from Amber, telling a love story that crosses faith and language. Name the film.
questions.explanation: Jodhaa Akbar dramatises the marriage of Akbar to the Kachhwaha princess from Amber, with extensive Persian court detail.

questions.question: Akbar's reign saw a Maktab Khana, a translation bureau, where Sanskrit classics — the Mahabharata, the Ramayana, the Bhagavata, the Yoga Vasishtha — were rendered into the court language. The Persian Mahabharata that came out of this bureau was given a name meaning the Book of War. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Razmnama, completed in the 1580s under Akbar, is the great Persian translation of the Mahabharata, lavishly illustrated.

questions.question: In the Persian-derived vocabulary of Mughal architecture, this is the great vaulted hall, open on one side, that you see fronting Iranian mosques and tombs from Isfahan to Agra. The Taj's central facade is essentially a giant one. What is this architectural element called?
questions.explanation: The iwan, a Persian invention, became a defining feature of Indo-Islamic mosques, tombs and palaces.

questions.question: Framing the great iwan of a Mughal tomb or mosque you almost always find a rectangular portal screen, often inlaid with calligraphy and pietra dura — a Persian device that gives the facade its monumental scale. What is this rectangular framing portal called?
questions.explanation: The pishtaq frames the iwan; the Taj Mahal's south face is dominated by an enormous calligraphy-rimmed pishtaq.

questions.question: A defining feature of mature Mughal tombs from Humayun's onwards: an inner shell that gives the chamber a comfortable interior height, and an outer shell that soars high enough to dominate the skyline. What is this two-layered Persian-style dome called?
questions.explanation: The double dome was perfected in Timurid Central Asia and reached India with Humayun's Tomb in the 1570s.

questions.question: In Lucknow's Husainabad complex, Muhammad Ali Shah built a smaller and more delicately decorated imambara than his predecessor Asaf-ud-Daula's giant — a building full of chandeliers, mirrors and silver tazias used in the Muharram processions of this Persian-influenced Shia court. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Chota Imambara, built in 1838, served both as a congregation hall and as a mausoleum for Muhammad Ali Shah.

questions.question: Within the Awadhi court the Persian word for a closed, curtained vehicle came to mean both a four-poster bed and the ceremonial palanquin in which a Shia mourner is carried. Around the time of Muharram, every neighbourhood of Lucknow puts out one of these. Which Persian-origin word?
questions.explanation: Taziya, from the Persian ta'ziyeh, refers in India to the model tombs and Muharram processions central to Shia Awadhi practice.

questions.question: Sitting in Persian gardens and Lutyens' Delhi alike, this Hindi word for a garden — also surviving in place names like Lalbagh in Bangalore and Karol Bagh in Delhi — came straight from Persian. What is the word?
questions.explanation: Bagh, Persian for garden, lives on in Indian place names from Shalimar Bagh to Lal Bagh.

questions.question: A slow-cooked breakfast stew of meat and bone marrow, eaten with naan or sheermal in old Delhi and Lucknow — its very name is Persian for trotters. What is the dish?
questions.explanation: Paya means foot or trotter in Persian and Urdu; the breakfast paya of Delhi and Lucknow descends from Persian slow-cooked stews.

questions.question: The Indian wedding-feast bread served straight out of the tandoor — soft, leavened, often shaped like a teardrop. Its very name is the Persian word for bread. Name it.
questions.explanation: Naan simply means bread in Persian; in India it now denotes the leavened tandoor flatbread.

questions.question: When Humayun was driven out of India in 1540 by Sher Shah Suri, he spent years in exile at the court of which Persian shah, who not only restored him to his throne with Persian troops but also sent back with him the artists who would seed Mughal painting?
questions.explanation: Shah Tahmasp I of the Safavid dynasty hosted Humayun in Tabriz and sent him back to India with troops and master painters.
